title: Arjuna's vow
hookLine: Karna still lives, Yudhishthira lashes out, and Arjuna reaches for his sword
carry: dharma upholds life; truth serves it

cards: Wounded and ashamed, Yudhishthira has been carried back to the Pandava camp. Then Arjuna and Krishna ride in from the field, and his face lights up. They've come, he thinks, to tell him Karna is dead.
They haven't. Karna is still out there. And the gentle eldest brother, sore from his defeat, turns on Arjuna with words he can't take back.
If you can't kill Karna, he says, in effect, give your bow Gandiva to someone who can. Arjuna's hand goes to his sword.

teach.b: Arjuna, the epic says, had made a secret vow: whoever told him to give his bow to another, he would kill. Now his own brother has said it. Keep the vow, and he kills Yudhishthira.
Break it, and he breaks his word. Krishna steps between them and asks a harder question: what is truth, really? He tells two stories.
An ascetic named Kaushika had vowed always to speak the truth. Robbers asked him which way some travelers had run to hide, and he told them.

The travelers were killed, and the epic says Kaushika suffered for that truthful answer. And a hunter named Balaka killed a creature that was about to destroy all living things, and was honored for it.
In Krishna's telling, truth is weighed by what it does to living beings, not only by the letter of a promise.
Hindu teachers often explain the word dharma from its root, dhri, to hold up: dharma is what upholds living beings, and truth serves it. Then he offers a way through.
For a man like Yudhishthira, he says, to be spoken to with contempt is a kind of death. So Arjuna speaks harshly to his brother, and keeps his vow without a drop of blood. At once he's sorry.
The brothers weep, and Yudhishthira blesses him.
Then Arjuna rides out again toward Karna, the quarrel healed. This week ends with a family pulled back from the edge.

how: Krishna's stories of Kaushika and Balaka from the Karna Parva are cited in Hindu discussions of dharma when truthfulness and harm pull in different directions, and the brothers' quarrel is retold in readings and serials of the epic.

o: the enemy still on the field while the brothers quarrel
the hunter Krishna praises for saving living beings
the brother who tells Arjuna to give his bow away

s: Yudhishthira thought Arjuna had come to report Karna's death
his joy turned to anger when he learned Karna still lived.
Krishna told Arjuna to keep his vow by killing his brother
he asked what truth really is, and found a way to keep the vow without blood.
in Krishna's story, Kaushika was praised for his truthful answer to the robbers
the travelers died, and the epic says Kaushika suffered for it.

games.q: you're Arjuna. you vowed to kill anyone who told you to give up your bow, and your own brother just said it. what do you do?
o: keep the vow to the letter.
break the vow and say nothing.
listen to Krishna, and find what the vow is really for.
games.why: Krishna teaches that truth is weighed by its effect on living beings; Arjuna speaks harshly to Yudhishthira instead, and the brothers make peace.

practice: Bring to mind a rule you keep, a line you never cross, and ask it Krishna's question: what life are you protecting? Let the question rest with the breath, without a quick answer.
If someone close to you spoke sharply this week, you can let their face come to mind, or hold them in prayer if you pray.

wordCard.voice: Karna. Still alive on the field, while the brothers who must face him nearly tear each other apart. So far: Karna's command, the crow, the promise, the quarrel.

orig.note: truth: what Krishna asks Arjuna to weigh, not only keep word for word.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma upholds life; truth serves it. A vow kept, and nobody harmed. Day eight hundred forty, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Karna Parva, Yudhishthira's rebuke of Arjuna, Arjuna's vow about Gandiva, Krishna's stories of Kaushika and Balaka, and the reconciliation
